name: SS-31
lead: SS-31, also called elamipretide (brand name Forzinity), is a synthetic mitochondria-targeted tetrapeptide developed by Stealth BioTherapeutics.[1][2] It binds cardiolipin, a phospholipid found on the inner mitochondrial membrane, and is given by subcutaneous injection as the hydrochloride salt.[1] In September 2025 the US Food and Drug Administration granted it accelerated approval, as a first-in-class medicine, for improving muscle strength in people with Barth syndrome who weigh at least 30 kg; Barth syndrome is a rare, life-threatening mitochondrial disease that mostly affects males.[1][2]

Before that approval it was studied in primary mitochondrial myopathy, heart failure, age-related macular degeneration and other conditions, with mixed results.[3][4][5] Its approval concerns one rare disease. It has not been approved for general anti-ageing, energy or appearance purposes, and no published trial has tested it in healthy people for those goals.

Outside clinical development, SS-31 circulates in peptide-using communities as a research chemical, where it is promoted for energy and longevity. Material sold this way is unregulated, and the clinical safety data come from supervised trials of the pharmaceutical product in patients with disease.
infobox: Rx-only for the approved indication; vendor products sold as research chemicals

paras: Elamipretide is indicated to improve muscle strength in people with Barth syndrome weighing at least 30 kg.[1] Barth syndrome typically begins with severe heart failure in infancy and, in those who survive to adolescence and adulthood, causes fatigue, poor stamina and exercise intolerance.[1] Grokipedia describes the cause as mutations in the TAFAZZIN gene, which impair remodelling of cardiolipin, and says the approval rested on improvement in knee extensor muscle strength as a surrogate endpoint reasonably likely to predict clinical benefit.[2] The FDA granted priority review and rare pediatric disease designations, and accelerated approval to Stealth BioTherapeutics.[1]
Wikipedia notes elamipretide has also been researched in heart failure, macular degeneration, diabetic foot ulcers and hypertension, but is approved only for Barth syndrome.[1]

SS-31 is described as a first-in-class cardiolipin-protective compound. A decline in cellular energy is common in ageing, and a 2014 paper in the British Journal of Pharmacology proposed that restoring mitochondrial bioenergetics could offer a common approach to age-associated diseases, with SS-31 binding cardiolipin to preserve it.[6] A 2013 paper in the Journal of the American Society of Nephrology reported that SS-31 re-energised ischaemic mitochondria through interaction with cardiolipin, and a 2011 paper reported that it accelerated ATP recovery and reduced ischaemic kidney injury in animals.[7][8] Other work describes targeting cardiolipin and the cytochrome c/cardiolipin complex to promote electron transport and optimise ATP synthesis.[9] The proposed result is more efficient electron transport and less reactive oxygen species production, though some reviewers question how far the free-radical theory of ageing explains the effects.[10][11]

A 2025 review covers the structure, mechanism of action and therapeutic potential of elamipretide,[12] and a 2022 review in Heart Failure Reviews discusses targeting mitochondrial dysfunction with it in heart failure.[3]

Animal and cell studies report effects in several settings. A 2011 Journal of the American College of Cardiology paper described a mitochondria-targeted antioxidant peptide ameliorating hypertensive cardiomyopathy,[13] and a 2016 Kidney International paper reported that protecting mitochondria prevented high-fat-diet-induced glomerulopathy and tubular injury.[14] In mice, SS-31 improved mitochondrial dysfunction and memory impairment caused by lipopolysaccharide,[15] and a 2021 GeroScience paper reported that it attenuated age-associated post-translational modifications of heart proteins.[16] Reviews also discuss mitochondrial dysfunction in kidney disease[17] and age-related macular degeneration,[18] and a systematic review notes impaired wound healing as an area where oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction are being targeted.[19] These are preclinical findings and do not establish cosmetic benefit.

Barth syndrome. TAZPOWER was a 28-week randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial followed by a 168-week open-label extension; a 2024 report of the extension evaluated long-term efficacy and safety, and a 2023 analysis examined responders using hierarchical clustering.[20][21] Grokipedia reports that the crossover trial showed a 27 percent increase in cardiac stroke volume over placebo and gains in 6-minute walk distance, and that the extension found no new safety signals.[2] A phase 4 trial and a paediatric pharmacokinetic study are registered.[22][23]

Primary mitochondrial myopathy. The MMPOWER-3 randomised phase 3 trial in adults with primary mitochondrial myopathy was published in Neurology in 2023;[24] Grokipedia reports that it did not meet its primary endpoints on the 6-minute walk test or fatigue scores, while a post hoc genotype-specific analysis suggested possible benefit in patients with mtDNA replisome disorders.[2][25] A further phase 3 study in primary mitochondrial disease from nuclear DNA mutations (n=102) has been completed, and an earlier open-label extension was terminated.[26][27]

Heart disease. A phase 2 trial in ST-elevation myocardial infarction reported that elamipretide diminished circulating HtrA2.[28] Grokipedia describes phase 2 studies in stable heart failure with a primary endpoint of left ventricular volume that was not significantly improved, and a registered trial in hospitalised heart failure (n=308) and in preserved ejection fraction (n=46).[2][29][30]

Eye disease. A phase 1 open-label study in intermediate age-related macular degeneration (n=40) has been completed, and the phase 3 ReNEW trial in dry AMD (n=313) is active but not recruiting.[31][32] A study of Friedreich ataxia (n=20) is also registered.[33]

No study was found testing SS-31 in healthy people for ageing, energy or appearance outcomes. A 2026 sports medicine review of approved and unapproved peptide therapies describes rapidly growing use of peptides outside regulated indications.[34]

The most common side effects identified in clinical trials are mild to moderate injection-site reactions.[1] Grokipedia reports that long-term extension studies found no new safety signals in Barth syndrome.[2] Long-term safety in other populations has not been fully established, and the data come from supervised trials of the pharmaceutical product, not from unregulated vendor material.

SS-31 emerged from work on mitochondria-targeted peptide antioxidants at Stealth BioTherapeutics, and a 2011 study of a mitochondria-targeted peptide in ischaemic kidney injury was an early publication in its literature.[8][13] It was developed as elamipretide through trials in mitochondrial myopathy, heart failure and eye disease.[3][24][31] The FDA approved it on 19 September 2025, according to Grokipedia, as the first therapy for Barth syndrome and the first mitochondria-targeted therapeutic to be approved.[1][2] An expanded access protocol for children with mitochondrial diseases has been available.[35]

In peptide-using communities, SS-31 is sold as a research chemical and promoted for mitochondrial support and energy. On T Nation in 2026, users describe stacks that pair SS-31 with weight-loss drugs such as retatrutide and with growth hormone secretagogues and MOTS-c, including a newcomer who lists SS-31 among compounds to begin with an initial weight-loss phase.[36][37] These are user posts and not clinical evidence; the posts reviewed contain no controlled data. No looksmax.org or Reddit material was identified.

timeline.event: A mitochondria-targeted peptide is reported to accelerate ATP recovery and reduce ischaemic kidney injury.[8]
SS-31 is reported to re-energise ischaemic mitochondria through interaction with cardiolipin.[7]
Phase II trial reports elamipretide diminishes circulating HtrA2 in myocardial infarction.[28]
MMPOWER-3 phase 3 trial in primary mitochondrial myopathy is published.[24]
168-week open-label extension of the TAZPOWER trial in Barth syndrome is reported.[20]
FDA grants accelerated approval of elamipretide (Forzinity) for Barth syndrome.[1][2]

lore.intro: On T Nation, SS-31 appears only in short 2026 posts about peptide stacks combining weight-loss drugs and growth hormone secretagogues; most threads that mention it are lists of compounds without discussion.[36][37]

claims.claim: SS-31 boosts mitochondrial energy and fights ageing
claims.believers: Peptide users describe it as a mitochondrial support compound to run alongside weight-loss and growth-hormone peptides.[36][37]
claims.experts: Preclinical studies report improved mitochondrial function in several models, but the human data are from patients with disease and no trial has tested it in healthy people for ageing or energy.[6][16][24]

claims.claim: Vendor SS-31 is equivalent to the approved drug
claims.believers: Community posts treat research-chemical SS-31 as the same compound used in the clinical trials.[36]
claims.experts: The approved product is Forzinity, a prescription injectable for Barth syndrome; the FDA's approval covers that product and indication only, and vendor material is unregulated.[1][2]

claims.claim: SS-31 is effective for mitochondrial disease
claims.believers: Patient communities and Stealth point to the Barth syndrome approval and expanded access reports of improved daily functioning.[2][35]
claims.experts: The Barth approval was accelerated and based on a surrogate endpoint; the MMPOWER-3 phase 3 trial in primary mitochondrial myopathy did not meet its primary endpoints, with a post hoc subgroup signal.[2][24][25]

claims.claim: SS-31 helps cosmetic skin anti-aging and wound healing
claims.believers: Some commentary links mitochondrial protection to skin repair and youthful appearance.[19]
claims.experts: A systematic review discusses targeting oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction in impaired wound healing, but no published trial has tested SS-31 for skin appearance.[19]
